newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Cracks appear among jubilant Euro Social Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Cracks appear among jubilant Euro Social Democrats.

text.p: European Social Democrats met in jubilant mood on Thursday after election wins in Britain and France but emerging cracks in the new face of Europe could not be camouflaged by the smiles.

With nine of the European Union's (EU) 15 countries now governed by the centre-left, the three-day congress began on a triumphant note, with France's newly victorious Lionel Jospin and Britain's Tony Blair leading the guest list.

But as Blair, the father of New Labour in Britain, prepared to tell the European Social Democratic Parties' Congress to modernise or die, other socialists were calling for the new Europe to distance itself more from right-wing politics to survive.

"There isn't much time to sell the concept of our vision of Europe to an ever increasingly sceptical people," the leader of the parliamentary group of the Party of European Socialists (PSE), Pauline Green, told the congress' 1,000 delegates.
"In three or five years' time, we don't want the verdict of Europe's people to be that we are just the same as the right when it comes to fine words and no action."

In a speech to be delivered on Friday, Blair was to tell his counterparts in Europe that they are destined for the scrap heap unless they follow his lead in rejecting outdated economic policies that stand in the way of job creation.
"Our task is not to go on fighting old battles but to show there is a third way, a way of marrying flexibility and security in a world of change," said Blair's speech, released ahead of delivery.
"If we can do that, our ideas become the mainstream -- the commonsense of our times.
"We must modernise or die... As long as we stay in tune with the changing world we will be trusted. As soon as we lose touch we will be out."
Blair's advocacy of flexible labour markets was likely to cause a few of the smiles at the congress in Malmo in southern Sweden to strain.

His stance is seen by many as more in line with the Christian Democrats than the socialists or social democrats. His talk of flexible labour markets is to critics a distasteful euphemism for low wages and easy hiring and firing.
"The right got a lot wrong but they were right about the need for flexible labour markets," Blair will say.
But others were not so tolerant of right wing policies.
Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said right wing politics were dead in the new, democratic Europe.

"People have turned their backs on right-wing experiments. We must meet the expectations that people around Europe place on us, to take responsibility for jobs, peace and stability and a better environment," said Persson.

With about 20 million people unemployed in the EU, employment was a key topic for the congress, which was seen as an ideal opportunity for EU socialists to harmonise their ideas ahead of a crucial summit in Amsterdam on June 16/17 to overhaul the EU.
"We have to come up with a common policy to fight unemployment," said Rudolf Scharping, leader of the Party of European Socialists. "We need to create jobs."
Other key issues to be discussed include education, the enviroment and EU enlargement.
Blair and Jospin were locked in their first bilateral talks on Thursday with both to address the congress on Friday.

Outside Malmo town hall where the leaders gathered for an official dinner, about 100 noisy protestors from pro-Kurdish and hardline left wing groups demonstrated, with one red banner that read: "Eurostrike for jobs. Smash bosses' EMU".
